newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's 'king of cocaine' in hospital.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's 'king of cocaine' in hospital.

text.p: Colombia's jailed "king of cocaine," Gilberto Rodriguez Orejuela, was taken to a hospital on Friday suffering from heart problems, prison officials said.

The former head of the once-mighty Cali drug cartel was transferred from his cell in the capital's top-security La Picota jail for what prison and hospital officials said was a scheduled check-up. But Colombian news media said the man nicknamed the chess player for his shrewd criminal brain was rushed in for emergency treatment after suffering a heart attack.

"Gilberto Rodriguez suffers from heart problems and high tension, and while these problems are not serious they must be looked after. This clinical check was planned at least a week ago," a spokeswoman for the national prison institute INPEC said.
He was taken to the San Ignacio hospital in downtown Bogota amid tight security, with scores of heavily armed police and prison officials providing an escort.
"Gilberto was not admitted to the emergency ward. This is a pre-planned check-up and he should be discharged within 24 hours," a hospital official who did not want to be identified told Reuters.

Rodriguez Orejuela's jailed brother Miguel, former Cali cartel No.2, also suffers from heart problems and undergoes regular medical checks. He also is in La Picota prison. Both were captured last year and have confessed to a string of drug-related crimes but have not yet been sentenced.

In their heyday, the brothers supplied 80 percent of the world's cocaine, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration says. Last month, the prestigious weekly political magazine Semana estimated Colombia's top drug lords were worth a total of more than $200 billion and the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers are thought to account for between $12 billion and $20 billion of that.

They have all the comforts of home at La Picota, including fine food, fresh-cut flowers, conjugal visits and cable TV. They were recently accused of running a campaign of bribery and threats from their cells against lawmakers who backed stiffer anti-drug laws in Congress, and U.S. authorities believe they continue to direct drug trafficking operations from behind bars.

In the latest insight into their cushy prison lifestyle, Colombian media, quoting unnamed sources, said the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers had been planning a New Year's Eve party with more than 400 guests, waiters and live bands. But they said the INPEC banned the party, limiting visitors to three per prisoner.
